reports.name: Shohei Ohtani
reports.published_report: The Statcast batting profile is almost uniformly elite: .413 xwOBA, 17.2% barrel rate, 93.4 mph average exit velocity, and a 14.3% walk rate that turns even the contact questions into a minor footnote. The contact questions are genuine, a 28.9% whiff rate that sits well below average, but a hitter putting that much force on contact at that walk rate absorbs a lot of strikeout variance without meaningful damage to the projection's .393 OBP. On the mound, a 2.71 xERA and 98.1 mph fastball with 2486 rpm of spin frame a pitcher who misses bats at a 30.4% whiff rate and holds barrels to just 3.8%. The whole thing hinges on health and innings load, which is the only scenario where both sides of this profile don't translate into something that belongs in a separate conversation from almost every other player at this level.

reports.name: James Wood
reports.published_report: The .428 xwOBA and 22.4% barrel rate both sit at the 100th percentile, and the .607 xSLG says the raw power is translating. The 29.6% strikeout rate is almost exactly the tax you pay for it, but what holds the profile together is the 17.1% walk rate: he's genuinely hard to put away, and a 22.5% chase rate confirms pitchers can't expand the zone to solve him. If the strikeout rate stays near where it is, this is a .266/.388/.530 line with 41 home runs, a true middle-of-the-order bat. If he ever finds enough in-zone contact to close the gap between his .277 xBA and his actual hit tool, the ceiling gets uncomfortable fast.

reports.name: Bobby Witt Jr.
reports.published_report: The xBA sits at .307, 99th percentile, and the contact quality underneath it is just as loud: 92.9 mph average exit velocity, 52.2% hard-hit rate, an xSLG of .518. Those three numbers describe a hitter who does genuine damage when he connects, and a 17.5% strikeout rate says he connects plenty. The one real tension in the profile is a 33.2% chase rate that lives in the bottom third of the league, meaning the raw contact talent is doing heavy lifting against a discipline number that could get exploited if pitchers find a consistent edge-and-off approach. If the chase rate stabilizes around its current level and doesn't climb, the projection's .283/.351/.471 with 45 stolen bags is an easy floor, not a ceiling.

reports.name: Pete Crow-Armstrong
reports.published_report: Thirty-two home runs and 39 steals in the same projection season is a combination that almost nobody produces, and the Statcast profile explains the mechanism. His 48.3% hard-hit rate pairs with a .357 xwOBA that reflects contact quality baked into where and how hard the ball is leaving the bat. The concern is specific: a 35.6% chase rate and 26.5% strikeout rate that rank near the bottom of the league, meaning the offensive ceiling depends on pitchers not solving him before he adjusts. If they do, you still have one of the fastest players in baseball at 29.5 ft/s and elite defense in center, which keeps the floor from cratering — but the 32-homer, 39-steal version only lives if the chase rate doesn't get him killed.

reports.name: Paul Skenes
reports.published_report: The xERA sits at 2.76 and the strikeout rate is 29.7%, and both are doing exactly what you'd expect from a guy holding opposing contact to a 6.1% barrel rate while walking just 5.6% of batters. That combination, miss bats, limit free passes, suppress damage when contact happens, is the cleanest formula in pitching, and Skenes executes all three. At 187.2 innings with 226 strikeouts and a 1.05 WHIP, the workload-plus-efficiency line is the kind that wins Cy Young votes. The one thing to watch is whether the 27.8% whiff rate, modest relative to the rest of the profile, firms up as hitters accumulate looks at the arsenal; if the chase rate at 33.9% starts to soften, the strikeout volume follows.

reports.name: Fernando Tatis Jr.
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile here has a real split personality. His 53.5% hard-hit rate puts him in rarefied air for pure contact quality, yet a 28.7% whiff rate bleeds enough of that value away that the xwOBA lands at .354, solid but not elite. The speed is genuine, 28.9 ft/s at the 90th percentile, and 38 projected steals tell you the legs are still a weapon even after everything. What the projection (.280/.351/.421) is really saying is that this is a plus-tools player whose floor keeps getting set by swing-and-miss, and if the whiff rate doesn't tighten from where it sits, the power (.421 SLG against an xSLG of .440) never fully arrives either.

reports.name: Elly De La Cruz
reports.published_report: The contact profile and the strikeout rate are pulling in opposite directions, and that's the whole argument. A 94.4 mph average exit velocity sits at the 99th percentile, the barrel rate is 14.9%, and yet a 27.4% strikeout rate drags the ceiling down — he's leaving runs on the field every time he swings through a pitch he could barrel. The .367 xwOBA says the underlying quality is genuinely elite when he makes contact, and the projection translates that into a .273/.347/.490 line with 27 home runs and 28 stolen bases, which is a legitimate star season. The profile hinges entirely on whether the strikeout rate stays at that level or creeps higher, because if the swing-and-miss ticks up, you lose plate appearances and the counting stats shrink fast, and what's left is a high-variance middle-of-the-order bat who is thrilling on his best nights and frustrating everywhere else.

reports.published_report: A 39.6 K% and a 2.07 xERA in the same Statcast profile is not a combination you find twice on a pitching staff, let alone twice in a generation. The 100.5 mph fastball with 2620 rpm spin explains the 37.5 Whiff% as well as anything can, and the .224 xwOBA against says the contact he does surrender goes nowhere. The one thread worth watching is the 6.4 BB%, which sits below truly elite command and is the variable that separates a Cy Young candidate from a guy who occasionally has to work out of trouble, because with that stuff, trouble rarely turns fatal. If the walks don't creep up and the 178.7 projected innings hold, the ValuCast 2.22 ERA reads as a reasonable translation of what the Statcast numbers are screaming.

reports.name: Riley Greene

He finds the zone well enough to run a .364 xwOBA, but his contact quality is doing real work that the strikeout rate tries to undo. The 14.3% barrel rate and 50.2% hard-hit rate say the damage is genuine when he connects, and the projection translating that into a .276/.365/.464 line over 668 PA is the reasonable middle ground between those competing forces. The profile holds if pitchers can't exploit the whiff rate to shrink his zone coverage; if they do, the walk rate stops compensating and the OBP drops with everything attached to it.

reports.name: Luis Arraez
reports.published_report: A 4.3% strikeout rate is not a typo. Arraez makes contact at a level that almost doesn't exist in modern baseball, and his 8.1% whiff rate is the cleanest expression of what he is: a bat-to-ball savant who wins by simply refusing to miss. The tension in the profile is that all that contact skill produces an xSLG of .372 and a barrel rate of 0.5%, meaning he needs his batted-ball luck to stay favorable because the raw power to carry a down year simply isn't there. ValuCast projects .317/.358/.434 across a full 686-PA season, and that line is believable for exactly one reason: the xBA sits at .286 because he hits the ball where it needs to go, even if he doesn't hit it hard. If the BABIP regresses sharply and he can't offset it with walks, a 6.0% BB% won't save him, and you're looking at a light-hitting first or second baseman who gives you a .270 average and not much else.

reports.name: Hunter Goodman
reports.published_report: 43 projected home runs from a catcher is the kind of number that makes you squint at the position line twice. reports.name: Jazz Chisholm Jr.
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile here is a puzzle with one very loud piece and one very damning one. His 90.8 mph average exit velocity grades well, and a 10.0% walk rate shows genuine patience, but a 31.5% whiff rate is quietly eating everything — the xBA sits at .210, and you can draw a straight line from that swing-and-miss problem to why the contact quality doesn't translate into actual batting average. Twenty-five home runs and 39 stolen bases in a full season is a legitimate power-speed threat, and that combination at second base or in the outfield carries real lineup value. The whole profile hinges on whether the strikeout rate, currently at 29.6%, compresses enough to let the hard contact show up in the box score; if it doesn't, you're looking at a .228 hitter whose speed and pop are backed by the exit velocity but whose on-base foundation is too thin to carry a lineup spot.

reports.name: Oneil Cruz
reports.published_report: The contact metrics and the power metrics don't belong to the same player, except they do. A 96.0 mph average exit velocity and 16.7% barrel rate that would make any evaluator drool sit right next to a 37.8% whiff rate and 34.6% K%, both at the bottom of the league. The question isn't whether Cruz can hit the ball hard; 59.2% hard-hit rate settles that. It's whether he makes contact often enough for that violence to matter, and the projection answer is .252/.339/.456 with 21 home runs and 31 stolen bases in 455 plate appearances: sometimes, and enough to be valuable, but this is a feast-or-famine profile that lives or dies by his at-bat quality in two-strike counts. If the chase rate at 32.4% creeps up and the walks at 10.6% dry up, the power doesn't disappear but the counting stats do, and you're left with a high-strikeout, low-average regular who costs you lineup continuity more than he builds it.

reports.name: Grant Taylor
reports.published_report: The xERA is 2.39 and the xwOBA is .241, both sitting at the 98th percentile, and that profile is backed by a 34.8% chase rate and a 33.2% strikeout rate that make the contact suppression look earned rather than lucky. Taylor runs 98.2 mph on his fastball with enough chase to miss bats at every quadrant of the zone, and the strikeout volume, 105 projected across 79.8 innings, is the engine that keeps that ERA figure credible. The one genuine tension in the profile is the walk rate: 8.4% is league-average-ish, and in high-leverage innings, that number matters more than it does buried in a rotation. If the command tightens, this is a lockdown closer; if it doesn't, he's a high-strikeout setup arm who earns his 12 projected saves by surviving the walks rather than eliminating them.

reports.name: Eury Pérez
reports.published_report: The fastball is 98.2 mph with 2665 rpm of spin, and that combination is what everything else in this profile is waiting on. The 28.0% strikeout rate is legitimate, the 28.8% whiff rate is above average, and the chase numbers are solid enough that when hitters do swing, he's getting them off balance. He's hitting the ball where it matters, an 11.4% barrel rate, rather than everywhere hard, which is a profile that sustains power without the raw thump to survive a miss. The projection's 23 home runs across 500 plate appearances is believable if he keeps finding the barrel at this rate; it unravels if pitchers find a way to expand his zone, because a 25.3% chase rate that looks disciplined today could drift upward as he gets more looks. Everyday corner infielder, probably leaning first base given the fielding percentile, with a .814 OPS ceiling that's less exciting than the xwOBA implies but more durable than the exit velo skeptics would expect.

reports.name: Theo Gillen
reports.peak_summary: Projection: low-end everyday regular with high risk. The current bat shape is impact over 265 A+ PA.
reports.published_report: Thirty-three stolen bases across AA & A+ before July, with a .423 OBP and 46 walks in 343 plate appearances, is a legitimately unusual combination for a 20-year-old. The .405 BABIP is the one number that deserves scrutiny: the raw line (.320/.423/.544) softens considerably when translated to MLB context, where the strikeout rate bumps to 26.7% and the ISO lands at .153, while MLB hitters collectively strike out at 22.0%. What Gillen actually has is elite on-base instincts and genuine speed; what he needs is for the contact quality to hold as pitchers get more sophisticated, because if the BABIP regresses hard and the strikeout rate stays elevated, the patience and stolen-base value may not carry enough weight on their own. The ceiling is a low-end everyday center fielder, and the floor is org depth, which is an unusually wide range for a kid running a 97th-percentile OBP right now.

reports.name: Jeremy Peña
reports.published_report: The xBA tells the loudest part of his story: .302, which puts him in rarified contact territory, and that grade holds up because his strikeout rate is a tidy 16.1%, not because he's running a soft contact scheme. The catch is that the underlying power infrastructure doesn't match — 87.5 mph average exit velocity and a 4.2% barrel rate are well below average, so the .438 xSLG is doing about as much work as it can with what's there, and the projection's .424 SLG reflects that ceiling rather honestly. What Peña actually is: a plus-contact, plus-speed shortstop (29.1 ft/s, 92nd percentile) who profiles as a .280-something hitter with 13-15 home runs and real stolen base value, not a middle-of-the-order threat. The whole thing hinges on that contact quality sustaining, because if the xBA regresses toward the exit velocity profile, the rest of the line gets thin fast.

reports.name: Sam Antonacci
reports.published_report: The contact quality here is a puzzle worth sitting with: a .291 xBA in the 94th percentile, a 15.7% whiff rate that almost nobody beats, and yet 87.5 mph average exit velocity in the bottom quarter of the league. He's making elite contact by frequency and placement, not by force, which is why the projection lands at .274/.363/.403 with 11 home runs rather than anything that reads like a power hitter's line. The 22 projected steals are believable given 28.3 ft/s sprint speed, and that combination of bat-to-ball and legs is what keeps the .766 OPS honest despite a 6.9% walk rate that will get exposed if pitchers start living in the zone and daring him to sell out. If the soft-contact profile keeps producing hits at the xBA rate, he's an everyday outfielder with real on-base value; if the league adjusts and the ground ball singles dry up, what's left is speed and a below-average walk rate on a rebuilding White Sox club.

If the walks tighten, he's a backend depth piece; if they don't, the floor and ceiling are the same thing.

reports.name: Michael Arroyo
reports.peak_summary: Projection: bench or platoon bat with low risk. The current bat shape is balanced over 297 AA PA.
reports.published_report: The contact is the easy part to trust: 56 strikeouts in 343 plate appearances across AAA & AA, which translates to a 19.9% whiff rate against an MLB average sitting at 22.0%, and a .295 batting average landing in the 89th percentile of the hitter pool. The harder question is whether the power follows. The ISO across AAA & AA is .180, but the MLB-equivalent translation pulls it back to .142, and the 15 stolen bases suggest his value runs through contact and speed more than through thump. If that translated ISO is where he settles, he's a bench or platoon bat who earns his spot by refusing to give at-bats away, and that's an honest outcome for a 21-year-old who already makes the ball-strike decision look easy.

reports.name: Mickey Moniak
reports.published_report: The .515 projected SLG and 11.6% barrel rate are genuinely loud for a guy whose xwOBA sits at .308 — that gap is the whole profile. The raw contact quality is real enough: 89.8 mph average exit velo, 43.9% hard-hit, and barrels in the 77th percentile all point to a hitter who does damage when he connects. The problem is a 41.9% chase rate that ranks in the 3rd percentile, which is the number that keeps xBA at .229 and walk rate at 5.4%, and that combination caps his floor badly. If the chase rate craters his batting average the way it threatens to, you're left with a power-only bench piece in a hitter's park rather than the everyday outfielder the projection imagines.

reports.name: Landen Roupp
reports.published_report: The contact profile is the whole argument: a 3.9% barrel rate and 28.8% hard-hit rate that put him in the 90s percentile-wise on both, meaning hitters are making weak contact even when they find the ball. His xERA sits at 3.41, but the projection ERA lands at 3.95 because a 10.3% walk rate is too high to ignore. He doesn't miss enough bats to carry those walks, a 24.4% strikeout rate with a whiff rate right at the league median, so the profile hinges entirely on that soft-contact suppression holding across a full season. If it does, he's a mid-rotation starter who consistently beats his surface ERA; if the contact management regresses even modestly, the walk rate has nowhere to hide.

reports.name: Josiah Hartshorn
reports.peak_summary: Projection: low-end everyday regular with medium risk. The current bat shape is impact over 190 A+ PA.
reports.published_report: The .395 OBP and 15 home runs across A+ & A at 19 years old command attention, but the whole thing collapses at the position. First base demands the bat carry the profile alone, and when you translate what he's doing to an MLB context, the ISO shrinks to .146 while the MLB average sits at .150, and the strikeout rate ticks up to 24.6%. The approach is genuine, 54 walks against 74 strikeouts in 367 PA is a real skill, and the 15% walk rate is the kind of discipline that usually survives the climb. But if the raw power doesn't grow into something well above average, a low-end regular at first is probably the ceiling, and the floor is a reserve.
